articles.title: Return Hubs in European Migration Policy
articles.title_zh: 欧洲移民政策中的遣返中心：一种具有系统性风险的残余工具
articles.description: A Residual Instrument with Systemic RisksThe EU Return Regulation creates a legal basis for transferring individuals subject to enforceable return decisions to third countries willing to accept them, even where they have no prior connection to that country. This makes so-called return hubs an increasingly likely prospect. The political appeal is clear: return hubs offer governments a visible way to demonstrate enforcement at a moment when the EU Pact on Migration and Asylum depends on credible implementation. But political salience should not be mistaken for operational effectiveness. European precedents and recent US experience suggest that transfers to remote third countries are likely to remain marginal, expensive and dependent on tenuous bargains. Return hubs may play a limited role for a small group of people who are otherwise difficult or impossible to remove, but they are not a general solution to low return rates. Their value should be judged by their ability to produce sustainable outcomes that cannot be achieved through the core return system. Without strict tests of additionality, propor­tionality and rights protection, they may make the wider return system harder, not easier, to fix.
articles.summary_zh: 欧盟遣返条例为将面临可执行遣返决定的个人转移至愿意接收的第三国提供了法律依据，即使这些人与该国没有先前联系，这使得所谓的遣返中心成为日益可能的前景。其政治吸引力显而易见：在欧盟移民与庇护公约依赖可信实施之际，遣返中心为政府提供了一种可见的执法展示方式。然而，政治显著性不应被误认为操作有效性。欧洲先例和美国近期经验表明，向遥远第三国的转移可能仍将边缘化、成本高昂且依赖脆弱的交易。遣返中心可能对少数难以或无法通过常规方式遣返的人发挥有限作用，但并非解决低遣返率的普遍方案。其价值应通过能否产生核心遣返系统无法实现的可持续成果来判断。若缺乏附加性、相称性和权利保护的严格检验，遣返中心可能使整个遣返系统更难修复。

articles.title_zh: 界定“白水区”：将寒冷海域作为海上行动秩序的特殊类别
articles.description: Cold Seas as a Distinct Category for the Operational Ordering of the Maritime Domain
articles.summary_zh: 本文提出将“白水区”作为海上行动秩序中的一个独特类别，以应对寒冷海域（如北极及亚北极地区）日益增长的战略重要性。作者认为，传统海上区域划分（如蓝水、绿水、棕水）未能充分反映寒冷海域在物理环境、航行条件、冰情变化及军事行动上的特殊性。文章系统分析了寒冷海域对舰船性能、传感器效能、后勤保障及人员操作的影响，并论证了将“白水区”单列有助于优化作战规划、装备研发与国际规则制定。通过引入这一新概念，作者旨在为海军战略家、政策制定者及国际海事组织提供更精确的分析框架，以应对气候变化导致冰层融化所带来的新航道与安全挑战，从而提升寒冷海域行动的有效性与安全性。

articles.title: The failed coup and Turkey’s path towards autocracy
articles.title_zh: 未遂政变与土耳其的威权化之路
articles.description: On 15 July 2016, factions within the Turkish military attempted to overthrow President Recep Tayyip Erdoğan and the government. The coup failed due to resistance from the public, opposition from the political leadership and divisions within the army itself. For Erdoğan, this presented a valuable political opportunity. Citing the need to avert further danger, he initiated far-reaching purges across the state apparatus and began a fundamental restructuring of the political system. Purges and institutional restructuring under a state of emergency On 21 July 2016, Parliament approved a state of emergency declared by the government. It remained in force until mid-July 2018. Erdoğan used it to carry out comprehensive purges across the state apparatus with 32 emergency decrees. Around 130,000 public-sector employees were dismissed. By the end of 2016, the authorities had arrested around 125,000 people, including 36,000 to 40,000 who were placed in pre-trial detention – with 149 journalists among them. By the end of 2022, the number of arrests and detentions in connection with the coup attempt had risen to around 332,000, with 4,000 judges and prosecutors losing their posts. Thousands of private schools, universities and foundations were closed by decree. A further 131 media companies were shut down, including 45 newspapers, 16 television stations, 23 radio stations and 3 news agencies. The authorities also revoked the passports of tens of thousands of people.  Extensive repression and the resulting climate of fear significantly restricted political competition and public debate. In this environment, the government initiated a restructuring of Turkey’s institutions. The decisive step was the constitutional referendum held in April 2017, in which a narrow majority voted to introduce a presidential system that significantly expanded the president’s powers. International election observers reported irregularities and concluded that the referendum was not free or fair. The legitimacy of the result remained controversial, not least because the Supreme Electoral Committee subsequently admitted around two million improperly stamped ballots on election night, thereby pushing the referendum to a narrow victory. The constitutional amendment strengthened executive power and largely concentrated it in the hands of the president. He was given extensive executive and appointment powers, while Parliament’s oversight and veto rights were restricted. In addition, the growing influence of the executive has weakened judicial independence. Numerous political scientists initially classified Turkey as a “competitive authoritarian” regime, with more recent analyses increasingly assessing it as an “autocracy”. International governance indices document this development. Turkey’s score in the Liberal Democracy Index nearly halved within a few years. Freedom House downgraded Turkey from “Partly Free” to “Not Free” in 2018. Since the state of emergency, the World Justice Project’s Rule of Law Index has also shown significant deficits in the rule of law and judicial independence. The economic consequences of autocratisation in Turkey Autocratisation was accompanied by a significant erosion of the central institutional framework of the Turkish economy. The weakening of democratic institutions, the rule of law and the protection of property rights, as well as the loss of central bank independence, increased uncertainties about economic policy. The growing concentration of power and the dismantling of institutional constraints on government action have negatively impacted the predictability of economic policy. This was reflected in key economic indicators, which pointed to a marked economic slowdown from 2016 onwards. In the first five years following the coup attempt, average annual real GDP growth fell from 6.5 in the preceding five-year period to 3.5 per cent, despite expansionary monetary and fiscal policies. At the same time, nominal GDP per capita fell from around $11,000 to $9,700. Foreign direct investment inflows also declined from an average of $15 billion to $11 billion. Export growth slowed from 5 to 3 per cent, while inflation rose from 7 to 14 per cent. The Turkish lira also depreciated significantly and became more volatile. There are currently no signs of a sustained economic recovery. The ongoing repression against the opposition party CHP and its mayors, as well as the government’s renewed efforts to amend the constitution to secure its hold on power, are increasing political instability and impacting the investment climate.
articles.summary_zh: 2016年7月15日，土耳其军方部分势力试图推翻总统埃尔多安政府，但因公众抵抗、政治领导层反对及军队内部分歧而失败。埃尔多安借此机会，以防范进一步危险为由，宣布紧急状态并实施大规模清洗，解雇约13万名公职人员，逮捕约33.2万人，关闭大量媒体、学校和非政府组织。2017年宪法公投在争议中通过，引入总统制，极大扩张总统权力，削弱议会监督和司法独立，导致土耳其被国际评估机构降级为“不自由”政权。威权化伴随经济制度框架的侵蚀，包括法治弱化、央行独立性丧失，导致经济增长放缓、通胀上升、里拉贬值和外资减少。文章认为，持续的镇压和政治不稳定进一步损害投资环境，短期内无复苏迹象。

articles.title: Defining the White Water Zone
articles.title_zh: 界定急流区：冷海作为海域行动秩序中的独特类别
articles.description: Cold Seas as a Distinct Category for the Operational Ordering of the Maritime Domain
articles.summary_zh: 本文提出将“冷海”视为海域行动秩序中的一个独特类别，以补充传统上对“蓝水”和“棕水”海域的划分。作者认为，随着北极冰层融化及大国竞争加剧，高纬度寒冷海域的战略重要性显著上升，但其环境条件（如极端低温、海冰动态、季节性光照）和操作挑战（如装备性能受限、通信导航干扰、人员生存风险）使其无法简单归入现有类别。文章主张建立“白水区”概念，以更精准地指导海军部署、装备研发和战术规划。通过案例分析和比较研究，作者论证了冷海在军事行动、威慑态势和盟友协调中的独特性，并呼吁政策制定者将冷海纳入正式的海域分类体系，以提升在高北地区的行动效能和战略响应能力。

articles.title: Why the Gulf Monarchies Will Not Turn Away from the United States Despite the Iran War
articles.title_zh: 为何海湾君主国不会因伊朗战争而疏远美国
articles.description: The signing on 7 August of the so-called Mecca Pact by Saudi Arabia, Türkiye and Pakistan again raises the question of whether the Gulf monarchies might seek to reduce their security dependence on the United States. The Gulf monarchies’ experience of the Iran war makes such a realignment appear plausible. Despite their decades-long partnership with Washington, they became targets of Iranian drone and missile attacks that caused considerable damage to the region’s energy infrastructure and severely disrupted energy exports, as the Strait of Hormuz was effectively closed. The Trump administration appears to have taken little account of their security interests. Nevertheless, three factors make an end to their close ties with Washington unlikely. Limits of realignment First, the Gulf monarchies have no viable alternative to the United States as a security guarantor. For all their differences in foreign and security policy, they share a common predicament: None of their other partners is willing or able to take Washington’s place. China has remained neutral during the war, Russia has maintained its close ties with Tehran, and Türkiye and Pakistan have provided no meaningful military assistance. Regional alliances such as the Mecca Pact are unlikely to alter this situation, as promises of assistance alone do not amount to reliable protection. Even the expansion of Emirati–Israeli military cooperation cannot replace the US security presence. Second, the Gulf monarchies’ military dependence on the United States goes far beyond the presence of US troops. US air-defence systems such as Patriot and THAAD have proved indispensable in countering Iranian attacks, while many of the Gulf states’ core military capabilities rely on US technology, spare parts, maintenance and training. These deep-rooted technical and institutional dependencies could only be reduced over decades and at considerable cost. Third, close economic ties also create path dependencies. China has become the Gulf states’ largest trading partner. Yet there is no evidence of a systematic move away from the US dollar in energy exports. Their sovereign wealth funds are estimated to have invested US$2 trillion in the United States alone. These economic interests provide the Gulf monarchies with an additional incentive to preserve stable relations with Washington, making any broader strategic realignment both costly and risky. Expanding channels of influence Against this backdrop, the war is unlikely to lead the Gulf monarchies to break with the US-led security order. Instead, they are more likely to seek greater influence within it. Saudi Arabia, the United Arab Emirates and Qatar, in particular, have cultivated close ties with policy-makers in Washington for decades and possess ample resources to expand them further. Alongside cultivating ties with President Donald Trump – whose businesses received around US$300 million from Gulf entities in 2025 alone – the Gulf monarchies could step up their lobbying efforts and draw more extensively on their contacts in Congress and across the US political and media landscape, including contacts on both sides of the political aisle. Above all, however, they are likely to deepen their economic ties with the United States. So far, the investment patterns of Gulf sovereign wealth funds show no sign of a fundamental shift away from the US market. In the first half of 2026, nearly half of their committed capital was allocated to deals in the United States. Partnerships with technology and financial companies such as Microsoft, Nvidia, Oracle and BlackRock offer more than commercial benefits: They also give influential US corporations an economic stake in stable relations with the Gulf states and may lend greater weight to Gulf interests in Washington. Whether the Gulf monarchies will become more effective at advancing their interests in Washington remains to be seen. Economic ties and privileged access do not guarantee that US policy will reflect their priorities. Moreover, differences among the Gulf states and regional rivalries have so far prevented them from presenting a united front in Washington. Processes such as Congress’s review of the proposed US–Saudi nuclear agreement, reached in late July, and its subsequent implementation could provide an early indication of how effective such influence can be. Yet even if their efforts yield only limited results, the lack of viable alternatives makes a fundamental break with the United States unlikely. Germany and its European partners should therefore not mistake the Gulf monarchies’ loss of confidence in Washington for a broader strategic realignment. For the Gulf monarchies, closer cooperation with Europe will remain a complement to their partnership with the United States rather than a substitute for it.
articles.summary_zh: 本文分析海湾君主国在伊朗战争背景下是否会减少对美国的依赖。尽管美国在战争中未充分顾及海湾国家安全利益，且伊朗无人机和导弹袭击对海湾能源设施造成严重破坏，但文章认为海湾国家不会与美国决裂。原因有三：首先，海湾国家没有替代美国的安全保障者，中国保持中立，俄罗斯与伊朗关系密切，土耳其和巴基斯坦未提供实质军事援助；其次，海湾国家军事上深度依赖美国技术、备件和维护，如爱国者和萨德防空系统；第三，经济联系形成路径依赖，海湾主权财富基金在美国投资约2万亿美元，能源出口仍以美元计价。相反，海湾国家将寻求在美国主导的安全秩序内扩大影响力，通过深化与美国的经济联系、游说华盛顿决策者，以及加强与美国科技和金融企业的合作，来维护自身利益。文章最后提醒欧洲国家，海湾国家对美国信心下降不等于战略转向，与欧洲的合作只是对美关系的补充而非替代。

These economic interests provide the Gulf monarchies with an additional incentive to preserve stable relations with Washington, making any broader strategic realignment both costly and risky. articles.description: Cold Seas as a Distinct Category for the Operational Ordering of the Maritime Domain
articles.summary_zh: 本文提出将“白水区”定义为海上领域操作排序中的一个独特类别，特指寒冷海域。作者认为，随着北极冰层融化及地缘政治竞争加剧，寒冷海域的战略重要性日益凸显，但现有海上行动分类未能充分反映其特殊挑战，如极端天气、冰情变化、航行限制及搜救难度等。文章主张建立“白水区”概念，以区别于传统的“蓝水”和“绿水”海域，从而更有效地指导海军部署、装备配置、训练标准及国际合作机制。通过案例分析，作者论证了该分类有助于提升寒冷海域的行动效率与安全，并为政策制定者提供新的分析框架，以应对气候变化带来的安全风险。文章强调，将寒冷海域单独归类是优化海上秩序、增强北极及亚北极地区战略韧性的必要步骤。

articles.title: The failed coup and Turkey’s path towards autocracy
articles.title_zh: 未遂政变与土耳其的威权化之路
articles.description: On 15 July 2016, factions within the Turkish military attempted to overthrow President Recep Tayyip Erdoğan and the government. The coup failed due to resistance from the public, opposition from the political leadership and divisions within the army itself. For Erdoğan, this presented a valuable political opportunity. Citing the need to avert further danger, he initiated far-reaching purges across the state apparatus and began a fundamental restructuring of the political system. Purges and institutional restructuring under a state of emergency On 21 July 2016, Parliament approved a state of emergency declared by the government. It remained in force until mid-July 2018. Erdoğan used it to carry out comprehensive purges across the state apparatus with 32 emergency decrees. Around 130,000 public-sector employees were dismissed. By the end of 2016, the authorities had arrested around 125,000 people, including 36,000 to 40,000 who were placed in pre-trial detention – with 149 journalists among them. By the end of 2022, the number of arrests and detentions in connection with the coup attempt had risen to around 332,000, with 4,000 judges and prosecutors losing their posts. Thousands of private schools, universities and foundations were closed by decree. A further 131 media companies were shut down, including 45 newspapers, 16 television stations, 23 radio stations and 3 news agencies. The authorities also revoked the passports of tens of thousands of people.  Extensive repression and the resulting climate of fear significantly restricted political competition and public debate. In this environment, the government initiated a restructuring of Turkey’s institutions. The decisive step was the constitutional referendum held in April 2017, in which a narrow majority voted to introduce a presidential system that significantly expanded the president’s powers. International election observers reported irregularities and concluded that the referendum was not free or fair. The legitimacy of the result remained controversial, not least because the Supreme Electoral Committee subsequently admitted around two million improperly stamped ballots on election night, thereby pushing the referendum to a narrow victory. The constitutional amendment strengthened executive power and largely concentrated it in the hands of the president. He was given extensive executive and appointment powers, while Parliament’s oversight and veto rights were restricted. In addition, the growing influence of the executive has weakened judicial independence. Numerous political scientists initially classified Turkey as a “competitive authoritarian” regime, with more recent analyses increasingly assessing it as an “autocracy”. International governance indices document this development. Turkey’s score in the Liberal Democracy Index nearly halved within a few years. Freedom House downgraded Turkey from “Partly Free” to “Not Free” in 2018. Since the state of emergency, the World Justice Project’s Rule of Law Index has also shown significant deficits in the rule of law and judicial independence. The economic consequences of autocratisation in Turkey Autocratisation was accompanied by a significant erosion of the central institutional framework of the Turkish economy. The weakening of democratic institutions, the rule of law and the protection of property rights, as well as the loss of central bank independence, increased uncertainties about economic policy. The growing concentration of power and the dismantling of institutional constraints on government action have negatively impacted the predictability of economic policy. This was reflected in key economic indicators, which pointed to a marked economic slowdown from 2016 onwards. In the first five years following the coup attempt, average annual real GDP growth fell from 6.5 in the preceding five-year period to 3.5 per cent, despite expansionary monetary and fiscal policies. At the same time, nominal GDP per capita fell from around $11,000 to $9,700. Foreign direct investment inflows also declined from an average of $15 billion to $11 billion. Export growth slowed from 5 to 3 per cent, while inflation rose from 7 to 14 per cent. The Turkish lira also depreciated significantly and became more volatile. There are currently no signs of a sustained economic recovery. The ongoing repression against the opposition party CHP and its mayors, as well as the government’s renewed efforts to amend the constitution to secure its hold on power, are increasing political instability and impacting the investment climate.

articles.summary_zh: 本文探讨了中等收入经济体在全球人工智能经济中的脆弱性，指出尽管这些国家积极参与AI发展，却高度依赖少数几个主导经济体，面临重大风险。文章认为，完全的技术独立对中等收入国家既不现实也不可取，关键在于建立“受管理的相互依存”关系。通过分析印度、中国与非洲的案例，作者提出中等收入经济体应通过多元化合作伙伴、加强区域合作、制定灵活的数字治理政策来降低依赖风险，同时利用自身市场规模和创新能力争取议价空间。文章强调，在AI地缘政治竞争加剧的背景下，中等收入国家需在开放与安全之间寻求平衡，避免被锁定在技术附庸地位，并呼吁国际社会建立更包容的AI治理框架，以保障发展中国家的数字主权和可持续发展空间。

articles.summary_zh: 本文提出将“白水区域”作为海洋领域作战秩序中的一个独立类别，以区别于传统的蓝水、绿水和棕水区域。作者认为，寒冷海域（如极地及高纬度海域）在物理环境、航行条件、军事行动限制及战略意义上具有独特性，现有分类无法充分涵盖其挑战与机遇。文章通过分析寒冷海域的冰情、气候、水文特征及对舰船、传感器和人员的影响，论证了建立“白水区域”分类的必要性。该分类有助于更精准地制定海军作战计划、装备研发及国际规则，并提升在北极航道竞争加剧背景下的战略响应能力。文中还探讨了白水区域与气候变化、地缘政治及安全治理的关联，强调其作为新兴海洋安全议题的重要性。

articles.title: The failed coup and Turkey’s path towards autocracy
articles.title_zh: 未遂政变与土耳其的威权化之路
articles.description: On 15 July 2016, factions within the Turkish military attempted to overthrow President Recep Tayyip Erdoğan and the government. The coup failed due to resistance from the public, opposition from the political leadership and divisions within the army itself. For Erdoğan, this presented a valuable political opportunity. Citing the need to avert further danger, he initiated far-reaching purges across the state apparatus and began a fundamental restructuring of the political system. Purges and institutional restructuring under a state of emergency On 21 July 2016, Parliament approved a state of emergency declared by the government. It remained in force until mid-July 2018. Erdoğan used it to carry out comprehensive purges across the state apparatus with 32 emergency decrees. Around 130,000 public-sector employees were dismissed. By the end of 2016, the authorities had arrested around 125,000 people, including 36,000 to 40,000 who were placed in pre-trial detention – with 149 journalists among them. By the end of 2022, the number of arrests and detentions in connection with the coup attempt had risen to around 332,000, with 4,000 judges and prosecutors losing their posts. Thousands of private schools, universities and foundations were closed by decree. A further 131 media companies were shut down, including 45 newspapers, 16 television stations, 23 radio stations and 3 news agencies. The authorities also revoked the passports of tens of thousands of people.  Extensive repression and the resulting climate of fear significantly restricted political competition and public debate. In this environment, the government initiated a restructuring of Turkey’s institutions. The decisive step was the constitutional referendum held in April 2017, in which a narrow majority voted to introduce a presidential system that significantly expanded the president’s powers. International election observers reported irregularities and concluded that the referendum was not free or fair. The legitimacy of the result remained controversial, not least because the Supreme Electoral Committee subsequently admitted around two million improperly stamped ballots on election night, thereby pushing the referendum to a narrow victory. The constitutional amendment strengthened executive power and largely concentrated it in the hands of the president. He was given extensive executive and appointment powers, while Parliament’s oversight and veto rights were restricted. In addition, the growing influence of the executive has weakened judicial independence. Numerous political scientists initially classified Turkey as a “competitive authoritarian” regime, with more recent analyses increasingly assessing it as an “autocracy”. International governance indices document this development. Turkey’s score in the Liberal Democracy Index nearly halved within a few years. Freedom House downgraded Turkey from “Partly Free” to “Not Free” in 2018. Since the state of emergency, the World Justice Project’s Rule of Law Index has also shown significant deficits in the rule of law and judicial independence. The economic consequences of autocratisation in Turkey Autocratisation was accompanied by a significant erosion of the central institutional framework of the Turkish economy. The weakening of democratic institutions, the rule of law and the protection of property rights, as well as the loss of central bank independence, increased uncertainties about economic policy. The growing concentration of power and the dismantling of institutional constraints on government action have negatively impacted the predictability of economic policy. This was reflected in key economic indicators, which pointed to a marked economic slowdown from 2016 onwards. In the first five years following the coup attempt, average annual real GDP growth fell from 6.5 in the preceding five-year period to 3.5 per cent, despite expansionary monetary and fiscal policies. At the same time, nominal GDP per capita fell from around $11,000 to $9,700. Foreign direct investment inflows also declined from an average of $15 billion to $11 billion. Export growth slowed from 5 to 3 per cent, while inflation rose from 7 to 14 per cent. The Turkish lira also depreciated significantly and became more volatile. There are currently no signs of a sustained economic recovery. The ongoing repression against the opposition party CHP and its mayors, as well as the government’s renewed efforts to amend the constitution to secure its hold on power, are increasing political instability and impacting the investment climate.

Money laundering, sanctions evasion and ransomware, terrorist financing, market manipulation, and sophisticated white-collar schemes are already benefitting from the expanding blockchain ecosystem used across the globe. What
articles.summary_zh: 本文探讨了区块链技术带来的双重影响：一方面为金融创新和经济发展提供机遇，另一方面却被犯罪分子利用从事洗钱、规避制裁、勒索软件攻击、恐怖主义融资、市场操纵及复杂白领犯罪等活动。随着区块链生态系统在全球范围内的扩展，这些非法行为日益猖獗，对国际金融体系构成严重威胁。文章强调，数字资产治理亟需加强，以应对加密金融犯罪带来的挑战。作者呼吁各国监管机构、国际组织和私营部门协同合作，建立有效的监管框架和执法机制，在促进技术创新与维护金融安全之间取得平衡，防止区块链技术成为犯罪活动的温床。

articles.title: Russian military spending soars, upending the Kremlin’s budget plans
articles.title_zh: 俄罗斯军费飙升，打乱克里姆林宫预算计划
articles.description: When Vladimir Putin takes the stage at a major public event, little is left to chance. Speeches, questions and answers are usually choreographed down to the smallest detail. Putin’s appearance at the Eastern Economic Forum in Vladivostok on September 3 was no exception. The plenary session began with a largely boilerplate speech by Putin on the socio-economic development of Russia’s Far East. But when Putin left the podium and returned to his seat on stage, the moderator immediately shifted the discussion to a different topic. He asked Putin about the state of the federal budget, pointing to the rapidly widening hole in Russian government finances. The choice of question was certainly no coincidence. The Kremlin apparently wanted to send a reassuring message about the budget. “There is nothing critical here,” Putin told the audience of economic and financial elites gathered in the plenary hall in Vladivostok. But Russia’s economic elites have plenty of reasons to be worried: The fiscal situation is deteriorating quickly as the costs of the war continue to soar. Newly released data on Russian spending in the first half of 2026 shows that military spending rose by 30 per cent compared with the same period last year, reaching 10.7 trillion rubles, or 4.7 per cent of projected GDP for 2026. Russia had originally planned to cut military spending this year. So far, the opposite is happening: If military spending continues at this pace, it will exceed 9 per cent of GDP by December, marking a new record in Russia’s post-Soviet history.  Fiscal pressures are increasing The unplanned growth of military spending is undoing the fiscal consolidation on which Russia’s budget for the current year was built. By the end of September, the Russian government is expected to present its budget plans for 2027. “Maybe we should start saving a little more?” the moderator suggested to Vladimir Putin at the Eastern Economic Forum, almost as if to pave the way for the president to justify painful new budget cuts. Putin responded that it’s not simply about cuts, but about spending rationally and with clear priorities, effectively laying the rhetorical groundwork for reductions that are increasingly likely to fall on the civilian parts of the budget. Budget cuts, however, will not free up enough funds to cover the increase in war costs. As revenues are not keeping pace, the higher military spending will translate into a higher budget deficit. By the end of July, budget data showed a deficit of 2.8 per cent of GDP – almost twice the original annual target. In recent years, Russia has used its National Wealth Fund to finance budget shortfalls, but liquid assets in the fund have dwindled to just 1.6 per cent of GDP. This means that the Russian Finance Ministry has to rely on new debt as its primary source of financing. However, domestic borrowing has become extremely expensive for Moscow. Against the backdrop of high public expenditure and concerns about higher inflation, interest rates on long-term Russian government bonds climbed to almost 17 per cent in July.  Doubts are not welcome in public The Kremlin has gone to great lengths to shield the Russian public from the impacts of the war, preserving a veneer of normality as the war rages in Ukraine. But in 2026, the strains of the war have become increasingly apparent. Ukrainian long-range strikes on refineries have caused a petrol shortage that the Kremlin has struggled to contain. Attacks on large warehouses have further exposed Russia’s vulnerability to Ukraine’s expanding long-range strike capabilities. Russia’s budget worries add to the mounting pressures that Putin is facing at home. On the sidelines of the Eastern Economic Forum in Vladivostok, another announcement was made that received little media attention: Russia’s state development bank VEB.RF presented a new chief economist. The position had previously been held by Andrei Klepach, a former deputy economy minister and one of Russia’s most prominent economists. Klepach had been dismissed after publicly warning about the mounting costs of the war and arguing that Russia was falling behind economically and technologically in a prolonged war of attrition. Klepach’s removal sent a clear signal that such doubts are not welcome in public debate. Those who remain unconvinced by Putin’s reassuring words are apparently better off keeping quiet. But silencing the doubters will not make the mounting costs of the war disappear. This analysis is based on data from the newly launched SWP Russian Budget Monitor. Click here for more information.
articles.summary_zh: 本文分析俄罗斯军费开支激增对联邦预算的冲击。2026年上半年，俄军费同比增长30%，达10.7万亿卢布，占全年预期GDP的4.7%，远超原定削减计划，年底或超GDP的9%，创后苏联时代新高。军费失控导致财政整顿失效，预算赤字至7月底已达GDP的2.8%，接近年度目标两倍。国家财富基金流动资产仅剩GDP的1.6%，财政部被迫依赖高成本国内借贷，长期国债利率升至近17%。为维持公众正常感，克里姆林宫压制异见，解雇了公开警告战争成本的经济学家克列帕奇，但此举无法消除财政压力。文章指出，预算危机叠加乌克兰远程打击引发的燃料短缺等问题，使普京面临日益严峻的国内挑战。

articles.title: Why the Gulf Monarchies Will Not Turn Away from the United States Despite the Iran War
articles.title_zh: 为何海湾君主国不会因伊朗战争而疏远美国
articles.description: The signing on 7 August of the so-called Mecca Pact by Saudi Arabia, Türkiye and Pakistan again raises the question of whether the Gulf monarchies might seek to reduce their security dependence on the United States. The Gulf monarchies’ experience of the Iran war makes such a realignment appear plausible. Despite their decades-long partnership with Washington, they became targets of Iranian drone and missile attacks that caused considerable damage to the region’s energy infrastructure and severely disrupted energy exports, as the Strait of Hormuz was effectively closed. The Trump administration appears to have taken little account of their security interests. Nevertheless, three factors make an end to their close ties with Washington unlikely. Limits of realignment First, the Gulf monarchies have no viable alternative to the United States as a security guarantor. For all their differences in foreign and security policy, they share a common predicament: None of their other partners is willing or able to take Washington’s place. China has remained neutral during the war, Russia has maintained its close ties with Tehran, and Türkiye and Pakistan have provided no meaningful military assistance. Regional alliances such as the Mecca Pact are unlikely to alter this situation, as promises of assistance alone do not amount to reliable protection. Even the expansion of Emirati–Israeli military cooperation cannot replace the US security presence. Second, the Gulf monarchies’ military dependence on the United States goes far beyond the presence of US troops. US air-defence systems such as Patriot and THAAD have proved indispensable in countering Iranian attacks, while many of the Gulf states’ core military capabilities rely on US technology, spare parts, maintenance and training. These deep-rooted technical and institutional dependencies could only be reduced over decades and at considerable cost. Third, close economic ties also create path dependencies. China has become the Gulf states’ largest trading partner. Yet there is no evidence of a systematic move away from the US dollar in energy exports. Their sovereign wealth funds are estimated to have invested US$2 trillion in the United States alone. These economic interests provide the Gulf monarchies with an additional incentive to preserve stable relations with Washington, making any broader strategic realignment both costly and risky. Expanding channels of influence Against this backdrop, the war is unlikely to lead the Gulf monarchies to break with the US-led security order. Instead, they are more likely to seek greater influence within it. Saudi Arabia, the United Arab Emirates and Qatar, in particular, have cultivated close ties with policy-makers in Washington for decades and possess ample resources to expand them further. Alongside cultivating ties with President Donald Trump – whose businesses received around US$300 million from Gulf entities in 2025 alone – the Gulf monarchies could step up their lobbying efforts and draw more extensively on their contacts in Congress and across the US political and media landscape, including contacts on both sides of the political aisle. Above all, however, they are likely to deepen their economic ties with the United States. So far, the investment patterns of Gulf sovereign wealth funds show no sign of a fundamental shift away from the US market. In the first half of 2026, nearly half of their committed capital was allocated to deals in the United States. Partnerships with technology and financial companies such as Microsoft, Nvidia, Oracle and BlackRock offer more than commercial benefits: They also give influential US corporations an economic stake in stable relations with the Gulf states and may lend greater weight to Gulf interests in Washington. Whether the Gulf monarchies will become more effective at advancing their interests in Washington remains to be seen. Economic ties and privileged access do not guarantee that US policy will reflect their priorities. Moreover, differences among the Gulf states and regional rivalries have so far prevented them from presenting a united front in Washington. Processes such as Congress’s review of the proposed US–Saudi nuclear agreement, reached in late July, and its subsequent implementation could provide an early indication of how effective such influence can be. Yet even if their efforts yield only limited results, the lack of viable alternatives makes a fundamental break with the United States unlikely. Germany and its European partners should therefore not mistake the Gulf monarchies’ loss of confidence in Washington for a broader strategic realignment. For the Gulf monarchies, closer cooperation with Europe will remain a complement to their partnership with the United States rather than a substitute for it.
articles.summary_zh: 本文分析海湾君主国在伊朗战争后是否会减少对美国的依赖。尽管战争期间美国未能充分保护其安全，海湾国家仍不太可能与美国决裂。原因有三：首先，没有其他大国能替代美国的安全保障角色，中国保持中立，俄罗斯与伊朗关系密切，土耳其和巴基斯坦未提供实质军事援助；其次，海湾国家军事上深度依赖美国技术、零部件和维护，这种依赖难以在短期内改变；第三，经济联系紧密，主权财富基金在美国投资约2万亿美元，且能源出口仍以美元计价。因此，海湾国家更可能通过深化与美国的经济联系和游说活动，在现有安全秩序内扩大影响力，而非寻求根本性战略转向。欧洲应认识到，海湾国家与欧洲的合作只是对美关系的补充，而非替代。

articles.title: Defining the White Water Zone
articles.title_zh: 界定白水区：冷海作为海上领域作战排序的独立类别
articles.description: Cold Seas as a Distinct Category for the Operational Ordering of the Maritime Domain
articles.summary_zh: 本文提出将“冷海”（Cold Seas）作为海上作战领域中的一个独立类别，以补充现有的“蓝水”与“绿水”分类体系。作者认为，当前的海域分类主要基于水深、距离和颜色隐喻，未能充分反映高纬度地区特有的环境挑战与战略意义。文章引入“白水区”（White Water Zone）概念，强调在极地及亚极地海域，冰情、低温、能见度低及通信受限等因素对海军行动、后勤保障和态势感知构成独特约束。通过分析冷海环境对舰船性能、武器系统及人员操作的影响，作者主张将冷海单独归类，以便更有效地进行任务规划、装备研发和国际规则制定。该分类不仅有助于提升北极及南极周边地区的军事应对能力，也为海上安全治理提供了新的分析框架，对国防政策制定者具有参考价值。

So far, the opposite is happening: If military spending continues at this pace, it will exceed 9 per cent of GDP by December, marking a new record in Russia’s post-Soviet history.  Fiscal pressures are increasing The unplanned growth of military spending is undoing the fiscal consolidation on which Russia’s budget for the current year was built. By the end of September, the Russian government is expected to present its budget plans for 2027. “Maybe we should start saving a little more?” the moderator suggested to Vladimir Putin at the Eastern Economic Forum, almost as if to pave the way for the president to justify painful new budget cuts. Putin responded that it’s not simply about cuts, but about spending rationally and with clear priorities, effectively laying the rhetorical groundwork for reductions that are increasingly likely to fall on the civilian parts of the budget. Budget cuts, however, will not free up enough funds to cover the increase in war costs. As revenues are not keeping pace, the higher military spending will translate into a higher budget deficit. By the end of July, budget data showed a deficit of 2.8 per cent of GDP – almost twice the original annual target. In recent years, Russia has used its National Wealth Fund to finance budget shortfalls, but liquid assets in the fund have dwindled to just 1.6 per cent of GDP. This means that the Russian Finance Ministry has to rely on new debt as its primary source of financing. However, domestic borrowing has become extremely expensive for Moscow. Against the backdrop of high public expenditure and concerns about higher inflation, interest rates on long-term Russian government bonds climbed to almost 17 per cent in July.  Doubts are not welcome in public The Kremlin has gone to great lengths to shield the Russian public from the impacts of the war, preserving a veneer of normality as the war rages in Ukraine. articles.title: Why the Gulf Monarchies Will Not Turn Away from the United States Despite the Iran War
articles.title_zh: 海湾君主国为何不会因伊朗战争而疏远美国
articles.description: The signing on 7 August of the so-called Mecca Pact by Saudi Arabia, Türkiye and Pakistan again raises the question of whether the Gulf monarchies might seek to reduce their security dependence on the United States. The Gulf monarchies’ experience of the Iran war makes such a realignment appear plausible. Despite their decades-long partnership with Washington, they became targets of Iranian drone and missile attacks that caused considerable damage to the region’s energy infrastructure and severely disrupted energy exports, as the Strait of Hormuz was effectively closed. The Trump administration appears to have taken little account of their security interests. Nevertheless, three factors make an end to their close ties with Washington unlikely. Limits of realignment First, the Gulf monarchies have no viable alternative to the United States as a security guarantor. For all their differences in foreign and security policy, they share a common predicament: None of their other partners is willing or able to take Washington’s place. China has remained neutral during the war, Russia has maintained its close ties with Tehran, and Türkiye and Pakistan have provided no meaningful military assistance. Regional alliances such as the Mecca Pact are unlikely to alter this situation, as promises of assistance alone do not amount to reliable protection. Even the expansion of Emirati–Israeli military cooperation cannot replace the US security presence. Second, the Gulf monarchies’ military dependence on the United States goes far beyond the presence of US troops. US air-defence systems such as Patriot and THAAD have proved indispensable in countering Iranian attacks, while many of the Gulf states’ core military capabilities rely on US technology, spare parts, maintenance and training. These deep-rooted technical and institutional dependencies could only be reduced over decades and at considerable cost. Third, close economic ties also create path dependencies. China has become the Gulf states’ largest trading partner. Yet there is no evidence of a systematic move away from the US dollar in energy exports. Their sovereign wealth funds are estimated to have invested US$2 trillion in the United States alone. These economic interests provide the Gulf monarchies with an additional incentive to preserve stable relations with Washington, making any broader strategic realignment both costly and risky. Expanding channels of influence Against this backdrop, the war is unlikely to lead the Gulf monarchies to break with the US-led security order. Instead, they are more likely to seek greater influence within it. Saudi Arabia, the United Arab Emirates and Qatar, in particular, have cultivated close ties with policy-makers in Washington for decades and possess ample resources to expand them further. Alongside cultivating ties with President Donald Trump – whose businesses received around US$300 million from Gulf entities in 2025 alone – the Gulf monarchies could step up their lobbying efforts and draw more extensively on their contacts in Congress and across the US political and media landscape, including contacts on both sides of the political aisle. Above all, however, they are likely to deepen their economic ties with the United States. So far, the investment patterns of Gulf sovereign wealth funds show no sign of a fundamental shift away from the US market. In the first half of 2026, nearly half of their committed capital was allocated to deals in the United States. Partnerships with technology and financial companies such as Microsoft, Nvidia, Oracle and BlackRock offer more than commercial benefits: They also give influential US corporations an economic stake in stable relations with the Gulf states and may lend greater weight to Gulf interests in Washington. Whether the Gulf monarchies will become more effective at advancing their interests in Washington remains to be seen. Economic ties and privileged access do not guarantee that US policy will reflect their priorities. Moreover, differences among the Gulf states and regional rivalries have so far prevented them from presenting a united front in Washington. Processes such as Congress’s review of the proposed US–Saudi nuclear agreement, reached in late July, and its subsequent implementation could provide an early indication of how effective such influence can be. Yet even if their efforts yield only limited results, the lack of viable alternatives makes a fundamental break with the United States unlikely. Germany and its European partners should therefore not mistake the Gulf monarchies’ loss of confidence in Washington for a broader strategic realignment. For the Gulf monarchies, closer cooperation with Europe will remain a complement to their partnership with the United States rather than a substitute for it.

articles.title: The failed coup and Turkey’s path towards autocracy
articles.title_zh: 未遂政变与土耳其的威权化之路
articles.description: On 15 July 2016, factions within the Turkish military attempted to overthrow President Recep Tayyip Erdoğan and the government. The coup failed due to resistance from the public, opposition from the political leadership and divisions within the army itself. For Erdoğan, this presented a valuable political opportunity. Citing the need to avert further danger, he initiated far-reaching purges across the state apparatus and began a fundamental restructuring of the political system. Purges and institutional restructuring under a state of emergency On 21 July 2016, Parliament approved a state of emergency declared by the government. It remained in force until mid-July 2018. Erdoğan used it to carry out comprehensive purges across the state apparatus with 32 emergency decrees. Around 130,000 public-sector employees were dismissed. By the end of 2016, the authorities had arrested around 125,000 people, including 36,000 to 40,000 who were placed in pre-trial detention – with 149 journalists among them. By the end of 2022, the number of arrests and detentions in connection with the coup attempt had risen to around 332,000, with 4,000 judges and prosecutors losing their posts. Thousands of private schools, universities and foundations were closed by decree. A further 131 media companies were shut down, including 45 newspapers, 16 television stations, 23 radio stations and 3 news agencies. The authorities also revoked the passports of tens of thousands of people.  Extensive repression and the resulting climate of fear significantly restricted political competition and public debate. In this environment, the government initiated a restructuring of Turkey’s institutions. The decisive step was the constitutional referendum held in April 2017, in which a narrow majority voted to introduce a presidential system that significantly expanded the president’s powers. International election observers reported irregularities and concluded that the referendum was not free or fair. The legitimacy of the result remained controversial, not least because the Supreme Electoral Committee subsequently admitted around two million improperly stamped ballots on election night, thereby pushing the referendum to a narrow victory. The constitutional amendment strengthened executive power and largely concentrated it in the hands of the president. He was given extensive executive and appointment powers, while Parliament’s oversight and veto rights were restricted. In addition, the growing influence of the executive has weakened judicial independence. Numerous political scientists initially classified Turkey as a “competitive authoritarian” regime, with more recent analyses increasingly assessing it as an “autocracy”. International governance indices document this development. Turkey’s score in the Liberal Democracy Index nearly halved within a few years. Freedom House downgraded Turkey from “Partly Free” to “Not Free” in 2018. Since the state of emergency, the World Justice Project’s Rule of Law Index has also shown significant deficits in the rule of law and judicial independence. The economic consequences of autocratisation in Turkey Autocratisation was accompanied by a significant erosion of the central institutional framework of the Turkish economy. The weakening of democratic institutions, the rule of law and the protection of property rights, as well as the loss of central bank independence, increased uncertainties about economic policy. The growing concentration of power and the dismantling of institutional constraints on government action have negatively impacted the predictability of economic policy. This was reflected in key economic indicators, which pointed to a marked economic slowdown from 2016 onwards. In the first five years following the coup attempt, average annual real GDP growth fell from 6.5 in the preceding five-year period to 3.5 per cent, despite expansionary monetary and fiscal policies. At the same time, nominal GDP per capita fell from around $11,000 to $9,700. Foreign direct investment inflows also declined from an average of $15 billion to $11 billion. Export growth slowed from 5 to 3 per cent, while inflation rose from 7 to 14 per cent. The Turkish lira also depreciated significantly and became more volatile. There are currently no signs of a sustained economic recovery. The ongoing repression against the opposition party CHP and its mayors, as well as the government’s renewed efforts to amend the constitution to secure its hold on power, are increasing political instability and impacting the investment climate.
articles.summary_zh: 2016年7月15日，土耳其军方部分派系试图推翻总统埃尔多安政府，但因公众抵抗、政治领导层反对及军队内部分歧而失败。埃尔多安借此机会，以防范进一步危险为由，宣布紧急状态并实施大规模清洗，约13万名公职人员被解职，数千名法官、记者等被捕，媒体和民间机构遭关闭。2017年宪法公投在争议中通过，引入总统制，大幅扩大总统权力，削弱议会监督和司法独立，导致土耳其被国际评估为“威权政权”。经济上，制度侵蚀削弱了法治和央行独立性，导致经济增长放缓、通胀上升、里拉贬值，外国直接投资减少。当前对反对派的持续镇压和修宪努力加剧了政治不稳定，影响投资环境。

Citing the need to avert further danger, he initiated far-reaching purges across the state apparatus and began a fundamental restructuring of the political system. Purges and institutional restructuring under a state of emergency On 21 July 2016, Parliament approved a state of emergency declared by the government. It remained in force until mid-July 2018. Erdoğan used it to carry out comprehensive purges across the state apparatus with 32 emergency decrees. Around 130,000 public-sector employees were dismissed. By the end of 2016, the authorities had arrested around 125,000 people, including 36,000 to 40,000 who were placed in pre-trial detention – with 149 journalists among them. By the end of 2022, the number of arrests and detentions in connection with the coup attempt had risen to around 332,000, with 4,000 judges and prosecutors losing their posts. Thousands of private schools, universities and foundations were closed by decree. A further 131 media companies were shut down, including 45 newspapers, 16 television stations, 23 radio stations and 3 news agencies. The authorities also revoked the passports of tens of thousands of people.  Extensive repression and the resulting climate of fear significantly restricted political competition and public debate. In this environment, the government initiated a restructuring of Turkey’s institutions. The decisive step was the constitutional referendum held in April 2017, in which a narrow majority voted to introduce a presidential system that significantly expanded the president’s powers. International election observers reported irregularities and concluded that the referendum was not free or fair. The legitimacy of the result remained controversial, not least because the Supreme Electoral Committee subsequently admitted around two million improperly stamped ballots on election night, thereby pushing the referendum to a narrow victory. The constitutional amendment strengthened executive power and largely concentrated it in the hands of the president. He was given extensive executive and appointment powers, while Parliament’s oversight and veto rights were restricted. In addition, the growing influence of the executive has weakened judicial independence. Numerous political scientists initially classified Turkey as a “competitive authoritarian” regime, with more recent analyses increasingly assessing it as an “autocracy”. International governance indices document this development. Turkey’s score in the Liberal Democracy Index nearly halved within a few years. Freedom House downgraded Turkey from “Partly Free” to “Not Free” in 2018. Since the state of emergency, the World Justice Project’s Rule of Law Index has also shown significant deficits in the rule of law and judicial independence. The economic consequences of autocratisation in Turkey Autocratisation was accompanied by a significant erosion of the central institutional framework of the Turkish economy. The weakening of democratic institutions, the rule of law and the protection of property rights, as well as the loss of central bank independence, increased uncertainties about economic policy. The growing concentration of power and the dismantling of institutional constraints on government action have negatively impacted the predictability of economic policy. This was reflected in key economic indicators, which pointed to a marked economic slowdown from 2016 onwards. In the first five years following the coup attempt, average annual real GDP growth fell from 6.5 in the preceding five-year period to 3.5 per cent, despite expansionary monetary and fiscal policies. At the same time, nominal GDP per capita fell from around $11,000 to $9,700. Foreign direct investment inflows also declined from an average of $15 billion to $11 billion. Export growth slowed from 5 to 3 per cent, while inflation rose from 7 to 14 per cent. The Turkish lira also depreciated significantly and became more volatile. There are currently no signs of a sustained economic recovery. The ongoing repression against the opposition party CHP and its mayors, as well as the government’s renewed efforts to amend the constitution to secure its hold on power, are increasing political instability and impacting the investment climate.
articles.summary_zh: 2016年7月15日，土耳其军方部分派系试图推翻总统埃尔多安政府，但因公众抵抗、政治领导层反对及军队内部分歧而失败。埃尔多安借此机会，以防范进一步危险为由，宣布紧急状态并实施大规模清洗，解雇约13万名公职人员，逮捕约33.2万人，关闭大量媒体、学校和非政府组织。2017年宪法公投在争议中通过，引入总统制，大幅扩大总统权力，削弱议会监督和司法独立，导致土耳其被国际指数降级为“不自由”或“威权政体”。威权化伴随经济制度框架的侵蚀，包括法治弱化、央行独立性丧失和政策不确定性上升，导致GDP增长放缓、通胀上升、货币贬值和外资减少。文章认为，持续的政治镇压和宪法修改努力加剧不稳定，损害投资环境，且无经济复苏迹象。

articles.title: Russian military spending soars, upending the Kremlin’s budget plans
articles.title_zh: 俄罗斯军费飙升，打乱克里姆林宫预算计划
articles.description: When Vladimir Putin takes the stage at a major public event, little is left to chance. Speeches, questions and answers are usually choreographed down to the smallest detail. Putin’s appearance at the Eastern Economic Forum in Vladivostok on September 3 was no exception. The plenary session began with a largely boilerplate speech by Putin on the socio-economic development of Russia’s Far East. But when Putin left the podium and returned to his seat on stage, the moderator immediately shifted the discussion to a different topic. He asked Putin about the state of the federal budget, pointing to the rapidly widening hole in Russian government finances. The choice of question was certainly no coincidence. The Kremlin apparently wanted to send a reassuring message about the budget. “There is nothing critical here,” Putin told the audience of economic and financial elites gathered in the plenary hall in Vladivostok. But Russia’s economic elites have plenty of reasons to be worried: The fiscal situation is deteriorating quickly as the costs of the war continue to soar. Newly released data on Russian spending in the first half of 2026 shows that military spending rose by 30 per cent compared with the same period last year, reaching 10.7 trillion rubles, or 4.7 per cent of projected GDP for 2026. Russia had originally planned to cut military spending this year. So far, the opposite is happening: If military spending continues at this pace, it will exceed 9 per cent of GDP by December, marking a new record in Russia’s post-Soviet history.  Fiscal pressures are increasing The unplanned growth of military spending is undoing the fiscal consolidation on which Russia’s budget for the current year was built. By the end of September, the Russian government is expected to present its budget plans for 2027. “Maybe we should start saving a little more?” the moderator suggested to Vladimir Putin at the Eastern Economic Forum, almost as if to pave the way for the president to justify painful new budget cuts. Putin responded that it’s not simply about cuts, but about spending rationally and with clear priorities, effectively laying the rhetorical groundwork for reductions that are increasingly likely to fall on the civilian parts of the budget. Budget cuts, however, will not free up enough funds to cover the increase in war costs. As revenues are not keeping pace, the higher military spending will translate into a higher budget deficit. By the end of July, budget data showed a deficit of 2.8 per cent of GDP – almost twice the original annual target. In recent years, Russia has used its National Wealth Fund to finance budget shortfalls, but liquid assets in the fund have dwindled to just 1.6 per cent of GDP. This means that the Russian Finance Ministry has to rely on new debt as its primary source of financing. However, domestic borrowing has become extremely expensive for Moscow. Against the backdrop of high public expenditure and concerns about higher inflation, interest rates on long-term Russian government bonds climbed to almost 17 per cent in July.  Doubts are not welcome in public The Kremlin has gone to great lengths to shield the Russian public from the impacts of the war, preserving a veneer of normality as the war rages in Ukraine. But in 2026, the strains of the war have become increasingly apparent. Ukrainian long-range strikes on refineries have caused a petrol shortage that the Kremlin has struggled to contain. Attacks on large warehouses have further exposed Russia’s vulnerability to Ukraine’s expanding long-range strike capabilities. Russia’s budget worries add to the mounting pressures that Putin is facing at home. On the sidelines of the Eastern Economic Forum in Vladivostok, another announcement was made that received little media attention: Russia’s state development bank VEB.RF presented a new chief economist. The position had previously been held by Andrei Klepach, a former deputy economy minister and one of Russia’s most prominent economists. Klepach had been dismissed after publicly warning about the mounting costs of the war and arguing that Russia was falling behind economically and technologically in a prolonged war of attrition. Klepach’s removal sent a clear signal that such doubts are not welcome in public debate. Those who remain unconvinced by Putin’s reassuring words are apparently better off keeping quiet. But silencing the doubters will not make the mounting costs of the war disappear. This analysis is based on data from the newly launched SWP Russian Budget Monitor. Click here for more information.
articles.summary_zh: 本文分析俄罗斯军费开支激增对联邦预算的冲击。2026年上半年，俄军费同比增长30%，达10.7万亿卢布，占2026年预期GDP的4.7%，远超原计划削减目标，若持续全年将超GDP的9%，创后苏联时代纪录。军费失控导致财政整顿失效，预算赤字已达GDP的2.8%，接近年度目标两倍。国家财富基金流动资产仅剩GDP的1.6%，财政部被迫依赖高成本国内借贷，长期国债利率升至近17%。为维持表面正常，克里姆林宫压制公开质疑，如解雇警告战争成本的经济学家克列帕奇，但此举无法掩盖经济压力。文章基于SWP俄罗斯预算监测数据，指出预算削减将主要落在民用领域，但不足以弥补军费缺口，财政可持续性面临严峻挑战。

articles.title: Why the Gulf Monarchies Will Not Turn Away from the United States Despite the Iran War
articles.title_zh: 海湾君主国为何不会因伊朗战争而疏远美国
articles.description: The signing on 7 August of the so-called Mecca Pact by Saudi Arabia, Türkiye and Pakistan again raises the question of whether the Gulf monarchies might seek to reduce their security dependence on the United States. The Gulf monarchies’ experience of the Iran war makes such a realignment appear plausible. Despite their decades-long partnership with Washington, they became targets of Iranian drone and missile attacks that caused considerable damage to the region’s energy infrastructure and severely disrupted energy exports, as the Strait of Hormuz was effectively closed. The Trump administration appears to have taken little account of their security interests. Nevertheless, three factors make an end to their close ties with Washington unlikely. Limits of realignment First, the Gulf monarchies have no viable alternative to the United States as a security guarantor. For all their differences in foreign and security policy, they share a common predicament: None of their other partners is willing or able to take Washington’s place. China has remained neutral during the war, Russia has maintained its close ties with Tehran, and Türkiye and Pakistan have provided no meaningful military assistance. Regional alliances such as the Mecca Pact are unlikely to alter this situation, as promises of assistance alone do not amount to reliable protection. Even the expansion of Emirati–Israeli military cooperation cannot replace the US security presence. Second, the Gulf monarchies’ military dependence on the United States goes far beyond the presence of US troops. US air-defence systems such as Patriot and THAAD have proved indispensable in countering Iranian attacks, while many of the Gulf states’ core military capabilities rely on US technology, spare parts, maintenance and training. These deep-rooted technical and institutional dependencies could only be reduced over decades and at considerable cost. Third, close economic ties also create path dependencies. China has become the Gulf states’ largest trading partner. Yet there is no evidence of a systematic move away from the US dollar in energy exports. Their sovereign wealth funds are estimated to have invested US$2 trillion in the United States alone. These economic interests provide the Gulf monarchies with an additional incentive to preserve stable relations with Washington, making any broader strategic realignment both costly and risky. Expanding channels of influence Against this backdrop, the war is unlikely to lead the Gulf monarchies to break with the US-led security order. Instead, they are more likely to seek greater influence within it. Saudi Arabia, the United Arab Emirates and Qatar, in particular, have cultivated close ties with policy-makers in Washington for decades and possess ample resources to expand them further. Alongside cultivating ties with President Donald Trump – whose businesses received around US$300 million from Gulf entities in 2025 alone – the Gulf monarchies could step up their lobbying efforts and draw more extensively on their contacts in Congress and across the US political and media landscape, including contacts on both sides of the political aisle. Above all, however, they are likely to deepen their economic ties with the United States. So far, the investment patterns of Gulf sovereign wealth funds show no sign of a fundamental shift away from the US market. In the first half of 2026, nearly half of their committed capital was allocated to deals in the United States. Partnerships with technology and financial companies such as Microsoft, Nvidia, Oracle and BlackRock offer more than commercial benefits: They also give influential US corporations an economic stake in stable relations with the Gulf states and may lend greater weight to Gulf interests in Washington. Whether the Gulf monarchies will become more effective at advancing their interests in Washington remains to be seen. Economic ties and privileged access do not guarantee that US policy will reflect their priorities. Moreover, differences among the Gulf states and regional rivalries have so far prevented them from presenting a united front in Washington. Processes such as Congress’s review of the proposed US–Saudi nuclear agreement, reached in late July, and its subsequent implementation could provide an early indication of how effective such influence can be. Yet even if their efforts yield only limited results, the lack of viable alternatives makes a fundamental break with the United States unlikely. Germany and its European partners should therefore not mistake the Gulf monarchies’ loss of confidence in Washington for a broader strategic realignment. For the Gulf monarchies, closer cooperation with Europe will remain a complement to their partnership with the United States rather than a substitute for it.
articles.summary_zh: 本文分析海湾君主国在伊朗战争背景下是否会减少对美国的依赖。尽管战争期间海湾国家遭受伊朗无人机和导弹袭击，能源设施受损，霍尔木兹海峡一度关闭，且特朗普政府未充分顾及它们的安全利益，但文章认为三国因素使它们难以与美国决裂：其一，海湾国家没有可行的安全替代者，中国保持中立，俄罗斯与伊朗关系密切，土耳其和巴基斯坦未提供实质军事援助，地区联盟如麦加协议无法提供可靠保护；其二，海湾国家军事上深度依赖美国，如爱国者和萨德防空系统，以及美制装备的零部件、维护和训练，这种依赖需数十年才能改变；其三，经济联系形成路径依赖，海湾主权财富基金在美投资约2万亿美元，能源出口仍以美元计价。因此，海湾国家更可能在美国主导的安全秩序内寻求更大影响力，通过深化经济联系、加强游说等方式影响美国政策，而非彻底转向。欧洲应理解海湾国家与美国的合作仍是核心，与欧洲的合作只是补充。

articles.title: Defining the White Water Zone
articles.title_zh: 界定白水区域：冷海作为海域作战秩序中的独立类别
articles.description: Cold Seas as a Distinct Category for the Operational Ordering of the Maritime Domain
articles.summary_zh: 本文提出将“冷海”（Cold Seas）作为海域作战秩序中的一个独立类别，以区别于传统意义上的“蓝水”与“棕水”区域。作者认为，随着极地冰层融化与高纬度地区战略价值上升，冷海区域在军事行动、航行规则与地缘政治博弈中呈现出独特挑战，现有分类无法充分涵盖其冰情、气候与基础设施限制。文章主张建立“白水区域”概念，以完善海上作战的态势感知与行动规划框架，并探讨其对北约、俄罗斯及其他北极利益相关方战略部署的影响。通过案例分析与概念推演，作者强调冷海需在政策与军事条令中获得专门关注，以应对未来潜在冲突与安全风险。

US air-defence systems such as Patriot and THAAD have proved indispensable in countering Iranian attacks, while many of the Gulf states’ core military capabilities rely on US technology, spare parts, maintenance and training. These deep-rooted technical and institutional dependencies could only be reduced over decades and at considerable cost. Third, close economic ties also create path dependencies. China has become the Gulf states’ largest trading partner. Yet there is no evidence of a systematic move away from the US dollar in energy exports. Their sovereign wealth funds are estimated to have invested US$2 trillion in the United States alone. These economic interests provide the Gulf monarchies with an additional incentive to preserve stable relations with Washington, making any broader strategic realignment both costly and risky. Expanding channels of influence Against this backdrop, the war is unlikely to lead the Gulf monarchies to break with the US-led security order. Instead, they are more likely to seek greater influence within it. Saudi Arabia, the United Arab Emirates and Qatar, in particular, have cultivated close ties with policy-makers in Washington for decades and possess ample resources to expand them further. Alongside cultivating ties with President Donald Trump – whose businesses received around US$300 million from Gulf entities in 2025 alone – the Gulf monarchies could step up their lobbying efforts and draw more extensively on their contacts in Congress and across the US political and media landscape, including contacts on both sides of the political aisle. Above all, however, they are likely to deepen their economic ties with the United States. So far, the investment patterns of Gulf sovereign wealth funds show no sign of a fundamental shift away from the US market. In the first half of 2026, nearly half of their committed capital was allocated to deals in the United States. Partnerships with technology and financial companies such as Microsoft, Nvidia, Oracle and BlackRock offer more than commercial benefits: They also give influential US corporations an economic stake in stable relations with the Gulf states and may lend greater weight to Gulf interests in Washington. Whether the Gulf monarchies will become more effective at advancing their interests in Washington remains to be seen. Economic ties and privileged access do not guarantee that US policy will reflect their priorities. Moreover, differences among the Gulf states and regional rivalries have so far prevented them from presenting a united front in Washington. Processes such as Congress’s review of the proposed US–Saudi nuclear agreement, reached in late July, and its subsequent implementation could provide an early indication of how effective such influence can be. Yet even if their efforts yield only limited results, the lack of viable alternatives makes a fundamental break with the United States unlikely. Germany and its European partners should therefore not mistake the Gulf monarchies’ loss of confidence in Washington for a broader strategic realignment. For the Gulf monarchies, closer cooperation with Europe will remain a complement to their partnership with the United States rather than a substitute for it.

articles.title: Defining the White Water Zone
articles.title_zh: 界定白水区域：作为海域作战秩序中独特类别的冷水海域
articles.description: Cold Seas as a Distinct Category for the Operational Ordering of the Maritime Domain
articles.summary_zh: 本文提出将“白水区域”（即冷水海域）作为海域作战秩序中的一个独特类别进行界定和分类。作者认为，传统上对海域的划分主要基于地理或法律标准，而忽视了环境条件（如低温、冰情、风暴等）对军事行动和海上安全的重大影响。文章主张，在高纬度地区，尤其是北极和南极周边海域，极端寒冷环境构成了独特的作战挑战，包括装备性能下降、人员生存风险增加、通信导航受限以及后勤补给困难等。因此，有必要在作战规划和国际海事秩序中单独设立“白水区域”类别，以更有效地指导军事部署、搜救行动和航行安全措施。该分类有助于提升对冷水海域特殊性的认识，并推动相关国家在战略规划和国际协作中采取针对性措施，确保在气候变化导致北极航道开放背景下，相关行动具备充分的准备与应对能力。

articles.title: The failed coup and Turkey’s path towards autocracy
articles.title_zh: 未遂政变与土耳其的威权化之路
articles.description: On 15 July 2016, factions within the Turkish military attempted to overthrow President Recep Tayyip Erdoğan and the government. The coup failed due to resistance from the public, opposition from the political leadership and divisions within the army itself. For Erdoğan, this presented a valuable political opportunity. Citing the need to avert further danger, he initiated far-reaching purges across the state apparatus and began a fundamental restructuring of the political system. Purges and institutional restructuring under a state of emergency On 21 July 2016, Parliament approved a state of emergency declared by the government. It remained in force until mid-July 2018. Erdoğan used it to carry out comprehensive purges across the state apparatus with 32 emergency decrees. Around 130,000 public-sector employees were dismissed. By the end of 2016, the authorities had arrested around 125,000 people, including 36,000 to 40,000 who were placed in pre-trial detention – with 149 journalists among them. By the end of 2022, the number of arrests and detentions in connection with the coup attempt had risen to around 332,000, with 4,000 judges and prosecutors losing their posts. Thousands of private schools, universities and foundations were closed by decree. A further 131 media companies were shut down, including 45 newspapers, 16 television stations, 23 radio stations and 3 news agencies. The authorities also revoked the passports of tens of thousands of people.  Extensive repression and the resulting climate of fear significantly restricted political competition and public debate. In this environment, the government initiated a restructuring of Turkey’s institutions. The decisive step was the constitutional referendum held in April 2017, in which a narrow majority voted to introduce a presidential system that significantly expanded the president’s powers. International election observers reported irregularities and concluded that the referendum was not free or fair. The legitimacy of the result remained controversial, not least because the Supreme Electoral Committee subsequently admitted around two million improperly stamped ballots on election night, thereby pushing the referendum to a narrow victory. The constitutional amendment strengthened executive power and largely concentrated it in the hands of the president. He was given extensive executive and appointment powers, while Parliament’s oversight and veto rights were restricted. In addition, the growing influence of the executive has weakened judicial independence. Numerous political scientists initially classified Turkey as a “competitive authoritarian” regime, with more recent analyses increasingly assessing it as an “autocracy”. International governance indices document this development. Turkey’s score in the Liberal Democracy Index nearly halved within a few years. Freedom House downgraded Turkey from “Partly Free” to “Not Free” in 2018. Since the state of emergency, the World Justice Project’s Rule of Law Index has also shown significant deficits in the rule of law and judicial independence. The economic consequences of autocratisation in Turkey Autocratisation was accompanied by a significant erosion of the central institutional framework of the Turkish economy. The weakening of democratic institutions, the rule of law and the protection of property rights, as well as the loss of central bank independence, increased uncertainties about economic policy. The growing concentration of power and the dismantling of institutional constraints on government action have negatively impacted the predictability of economic policy. This was reflected in key economic indicators, which pointed to a marked economic slowdown from 2016 onwards. In the first five years following the coup attempt, average annual real GDP growth fell from 6.5 in the preceding five-year period to 3.5 per cent, despite expansionary monetary and fiscal policies. At the same time, nominal GDP per capita fell from around $11,000 to $9,700. Foreign direct investment inflows also declined from an average of $15 billion to $11 billion. Export growth slowed from 5 to 3 per cent, while inflation rose from 7 to 14 per cent. The Turkish lira also depreciated significantly and became more volatile. There are currently no signs of a sustained economic recovery. The ongoing repression against the opposition party CHP and its mayors, as well as the government’s renewed efforts to amend the constitution to secure its hold on power, are increasing political instability and impacting the investment climate.
articles.summary_zh: 2016年7月15日，土耳其军方部分势力试图推翻总统埃尔多安政府，但未遂。埃尔多安借此机会，以安全为由实施紧急状态，进行大规模清洗和制度重构。约13万名公职人员被解职，至2022年底约33.2万人被捕或拘留，媒体、学校和非政府组织遭关闭。2017年宪法公投在争议中通过，确立总统制，极大扩张总统权力，削弱议会监督和司法独立，导致土耳其被国际评估为“威权政体”。威权化伴随经济制度框架的侵蚀，法治和央行独立性受损，经济不确定性上升，GDP增长放缓、通胀上升、里拉贬值，外资减少。当前对反对党的持续打压和修宪努力加剧政治不稳定，影响投资环境。

articles.title: Russian military spending soars, upending the Kremlin’s budget plans
articles.title_zh: 俄罗斯军费飙升，打乱克里姆林宫预算计划
articles.description: When Vladimir Putin takes the stage at a major public event, little is left to chance. Speeches, questions and answers are usually choreographed down to the smallest detail. Putin’s appearance at the Eastern Economic Forum in Vladivostok on September 3 was no exception. The plenary session began with a largely boilerplate speech by Putin on the socio-economic development of Russia’s Far East. But when Putin left the podium and returned to his seat on stage, the moderator immediately shifted the discussion to a different topic. He asked Putin about the state of the federal budget, pointing to the rapidly widening hole in Russian government finances. The choice of question was certainly no coincidence. The Kremlin apparently wanted to send a reassuring message about the budget. “There is nothing critical here,” Putin told the audience of economic and financial elites gathered in the plenary hall in Vladivostok. But Russia’s economic elites have plenty of reasons to be worried: The fiscal situation is deteriorating quickly as the costs of the war continue to soar. Newly released data on Russian spending in the first half of 2026 shows that military spending rose by 30 per cent compared with the same period last year, reaching 10.7 trillion rubles, or 4.7 per cent of projected GDP for 2026. Russia had originally planned to cut military spending this year. So far, the opposite is happening: If military spending continues at this pace, it will exceed 9 per cent of GDP by December, marking a new record in Russia’s post-Soviet history.  Fiscal pressures are increasing The unplanned growth of military spending is undoing the fiscal consolidation on which Russia’s budget for the current year was built. By the end of September, the Russian government is expected to present its budget plans for 2027. “Maybe we should start saving a little more?” the moderator suggested to Vladimir Putin at the Eastern Economic Forum, almost as if to pave the way for the president to justify painful new budget cuts. Putin responded that it’s not simply about cuts, but about spending rationally and with clear priorities, effectively laying the rhetorical groundwork for reductions that are increasingly likely to fall on the civilian parts of the budget. Budget cuts, however, will not free up enough funds to cover the increase in war costs. As revenues are not keeping pace, the higher military spending will translate into a higher budget deficit. By the end of July, budget data showed a deficit of 2.8 per cent of GDP – almost twice the original annual target. In recent years, Russia has used its National Wealth Fund to finance budget shortfalls, but liquid assets in the fund have dwindled to just 1.6 per cent of GDP. This means that the Russian Finance Ministry has to rely on new debt as its primary source of financing. However, domestic borrowing has become extremely expensive for Moscow. Against the backdrop of high public expenditure and concerns about higher inflation, interest rates on long-term Russian government bonds climbed to almost 17 per cent in July.  Doubts are not welcome in public The Kremlin has gone to great lengths to shield the Russian public from the impacts of the war, preserving a veneer of normality as the war rages in Ukraine. But in 2026, the strains of the war have become increasingly apparent. Ukrainian long-range strikes on refineries have caused a petrol shortage that the Kremlin has struggled to contain. Attacks on large warehouses have further exposed Russia’s vulnerability to Ukraine’s expanding long-range strike capabilities. Russia’s budget worries add to the mounting pressures that Putin is facing at home. On the sidelines of the Eastern Economic Forum in Vladivostok, another announcement was made that received little media attention: Russia’s state development bank VEB.RF presented a new chief economist. The position had previously been held by Andrei Klepach, a former deputy economy minister and one of Russia’s most prominent economists. Klepach had been dismissed after publicly warning about the mounting costs of the war and arguing that Russia was falling behind economically and technologically in a prolonged war of attrition. Klepach’s removal sent a clear signal that such doubts are not welcome in public debate. Those who remain unconvinced by Putin’s reassuring words are apparently better off keeping quiet. But silencing the doubters will not make the mounting costs of the war disappear. This analysis is based on data from the newly launched SWP Russian Budget Monitor. Click here for more information.
articles.summary_zh: 本文分析俄罗斯军费开支激增对联邦预算的冲击。2026年上半年，俄军费同比增长30%，达10.7万亿卢布，占2026年预期GDP的4.7%，远超原定削减计划，若持续全年将超GDP的9%，创后苏联时代新高。这导致财政整顿失效，预算赤字截至7月底已达GDP的2.8%，接近年度目标两倍。国家财富基金流动资产仅剩GDP的1.6%，财政部被迫依赖高成本国内借贷，长期国债利率升至近17%。为维持战争表象，克里姆林宫压制公开质疑，如解雇警告战争代价的经济学家克列帕奇，但此举无法掩盖经济压力。文章基于SWP俄罗斯预算监测数据，指出预算削减将主要落在民用领域，但不足以弥补军费缺口，财政前景严峻。

articles.title: Why the Gulf Monarchies Will Not Turn Away from the United States Despite the Iran War

Despite their decades-long partnership with Washington, they became targets of Iranian drone and missile attacks that caused considerable damage to the region’s energy infrastructure and severely disrupted energy exports, as the Strait of Hormuz was effectively closed. The Trump administration appears to have taken little account of their security interests. Nevertheless, three factors make an end to their close ties with Washington unlikely. Limits of realignment First, the Gulf monarchies have no viable alternative to the United States as a security guarantor. For all their differences in foreign and security policy, they share a common predicament: None of their other partners is willing or able to take Washington’s place. China has remained neutral during the war, Russia has maintained its close ties with Tehran, and Türkiye and Pakistan have provided no meaningful military assistance. Regional alliances such as the Mecca Pact are unlikely to alter this situation, as promises of assistance alone do not amount to reliable protection. Even the expansion of Emirati–Israeli military cooperation cannot replace the US security presence. Second, the Gulf monarchies’ military dependence on the United States goes far beyond the presence of US troops. US air-defence systems such as Patriot and THAAD have proved indispensable in countering Iranian attacks, while many of the Gulf states’ core military capabilities rely on US technology, spare parts, maintenance and training. These deep-rooted technical and institutional dependencies could only be reduced over decades and at considerable cost. Third, close economic ties also create path dependencies. China has become the Gulf states’ largest trading partner. Yet there is no evidence of a systematic move away from the US dollar in energy exports. Their sovereign wealth funds are estimated to have invested US$2 trillion in the United States alone. These economic interests provide the Gulf monarchies with an additional incentive to preserve stable relations with Washington, making any broader strategic realignment both costly and risky. Expanding channels of influence Against this backdrop, the war is unlikely to lead the Gulf monarchies to break with the US-led security order. Instead, they are more likely to seek greater influence within it. Saudi Arabia, the United Arab Emirates and Qatar, in particular, have cultivated close ties with policy-makers in Washington for decades and possess ample resources to expand them further. Alongside cultivating ties with President Donald Trump – whose businesses received around US$300 million from Gulf entities in 2025 alone – the Gulf monarchies could step up their lobbying efforts and draw more extensively on their contacts in Congress and across the US political and media landscape, including contacts on both sides of the political aisle. Above all, however, they are likely to deepen their economic ties with the United States. So far, the investment patterns of Gulf sovereign wealth funds show no sign of a fundamental shift away from the US market.
